story.headline: Oxford University Grants OpenAI Training Access to the Bodleian Library
story.summary: Oxford University has reached an agreement allowing OpenAI to train its artificial intelligence models on the historic collections of the Bodleian Library. The partnership provides the AI lab with vast archival text corpora to improve its reasoning and knowledge capabilities.

draft.body:
The University of Oxford has permitted ChatGPT developer OpenAI to train its artificial intelligence models on historical texts scanned from its Bodleian Library collections, according to internal university records obtained through freedom of information requests. The disclosure, first reported by [The Guardian](https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/sep/26/oxford-university-bodleian-library-open-ai-chat-gpt), confirms that scans digitized under an academic partnership have been directly fed into OpenAI's machine learning pipelines.

Oxford previously announced a five-year collaboration with OpenAI in March 2025, framed primarily as an initiative to digitize rare public domain works, roll out ChatGPT Edu across campus, and provide research funding, as outlined in the university's [official partnership announcement](https://www.bodleian.ox.ac.uk/about/media/oxford-and-openai-launch). However, public notices made no mention that the library materials would be fed directly into commercial model training.

[[FIG1]]

## The Scope of the Bodleian Library AI Training Data

Internal meeting minutes reveal that materials digitized by OpenAI have served to "populate the OpenAI training set," as reported by [The News International](https://www.thenews.com.pk/latest/1417727-oxford-gives-openai-access-to-bodleian-library-for-ai-training). By June 2025, approximately 125,000 page images from historical dissertations had been shared with OpenAI. The dissertations comprise 19th- and 20th-century PhD theses from European and American universities, while other texts scanned include a collection of 10,000 16th-century "broadside ballads" containing early modern song lyrics and musical notation.

University staff also evaluated other rare archival holdings for potential processing. These candidates included 18th-century Irish state papers, the private letters of novelist Marie Edgeworth, and Dorothy Hodgkin’s penicillin laboratory notebooks. Meeting notes also detailed discussions regarding a potential "Ask the Bod" conversational tool.

According to documentation on the [Bodleian Digitisation Research project](https://www.bodleian.ox.ac.uk/services/research-partnerships/digitisation-project), the library established five specific workstreams to test scaling digitisation throughput across its Weston Library imaging studio and its Collections Storage Facility in Swindon, which houses over 10 million items. The project is trialing optical character recognition and handwriting text recognition technologies, comparing traditional extraction against generative AI tools funded by OpenAI.

[[FIG2]]

## Internal Pushback and Oxford's Stance

Internal meeting minutes from the Bodleian governance committee record pushback from faculty and library staff. Members expressed worry regarding the reputational hazards of partnering with OpenAI, alongside the tension between AI's substantial computational power demands and Oxford's institutional sustainability goals.

A spokesperson for Oxford University defended the initiative, stating that the project focuses on out-of-copyright material and is "modest in scale." The university asserted that it had not hidden the machine-learning aspects of the project, with an Oxford spokesperson stating that while digitisation was the university's primary interest, staff had been open that the project would also contribute training data.

Oxford emphasized that the agreement is non-exclusive and that the Bodleian retains all ownership rights over the digital files. Scanned works are scheduled to be published openly online in the coming months, allowing researchers worldwide to read and study them without restriction.

## Academic Archives and the Race for Untapped Text

The Bodleian partnership reflects an industry-wide scramble for human-written, out-of-copyright text. Because the public internet has become crowded with synthetic and auto-generated copy, developers have turned to physical, often historical, book collections and obscure secondhand titles.

Other AI laboratories have pursued aggressive acquisition tactics. Anthropic spent tens of millions of dollars acquiring physical books, slicing off bindings for high-speed scanning before sending the paper to be pulped, though Anthropic stated it does not destroy antiquarian titles. Similar automated book-disassembly workflows have been documented at third-party facilities.

By contrast, Oxford confirmed that all Bodleian holdings remain fully intact. The collaboration functions under OpenAI's NextGenAI initiative, a $50 million academic program that includes US partners such as MIT, Caltech, the University of Michigan, and the Boston Public Library. Oxford remains the sole UK university participating in the consortium.

faq.q: Did Oxford University sell exclusive access to its library archives?
faq.a: No. Oxford confirmed that its agreement with OpenAI is non-exclusive, that the Bodleian retains full ownership of the digital scans, and that the digitized texts will be published freely online for the public.

faq.q: What specific collections have been scanned for OpenAI training?
faq.a: Transfers to OpenAI included 125,000 scanned images from 19th- and 20th-century dissertations, while 10,000 16th-century ballads were among the other texts scanned, with additional collections reviewed for future processing.

faq.q: Were any Bodleian Library books destroyed during scanning?
faq.a: No. Bodleian collections remain intact, unlike secondhand book acquisitions elsewhere that are pulped after scanning.
